concepts.name: Land Revenue (Kharaj) — Rate and Assessment Basis
key_dimensions: Rate fixed at 50% of produce — distinction from earlier sultans who levied lower rates
Shift from produce-based to area-based (biswa) measurement — significance of standardization
Whether the 50% rate applied to all land categories or had exemptions (e.g., khalisa vs. iqta lands)
UPSC trap: confusing Kharaj (land tax on Muslims vs. non-Muslims) with the general land revenue demand under Alauddin

concepts.name: Biswa System — Standardization of Land Measurement
key_dimensions: Introduction of biswa as a standard unit to replace variable local units — administrative rationale
Role of measurement (paimaish) in curbing evasion by intermediaries and village headmen (khuts/muqaddams)
Comparison with Akbar's later zabt system — similarities and differences in methodology
UPSC trap: attributing standardized measurement solely to Akbar, ignoring Alauddin's precedent

concepts.name: Suppression of Khuts, Muqaddams, and Chaudharis
key_dimensions: Who were khuts, muqaddams, and chaudharis — their traditional privileges and role as revenue intermediaries
Alauddin's policy of making them pay taxes like ordinary peasants — removal of concessions (chari, charai exemptions)
Use of harsh punishments (flogging, imprisonment) to enforce compliance — coercive vs. administrative logic
UPSC trap: mistaking suppression of these intermediaries as abolition of the zamindari-type structure altogether

concepts.name: Ghari (House Tax) and Charai (Grazing Tax)
key_dimensions: Nature of Ghari — tax on houses, applied uniformly to the Doab region
Nature of Charai — tax on milch cattle, intended to curb rural prosperity among intermediaries
Whether these were new taxes or enhanced versions of pre-existing levies — historiographical debate
UPSC trap: confusing Ghari and Charai as taxes on peasants only vs. specifically targeting rural elites (khuts/muqaddams)

concepts.name: Market Reforms (Shahna-i-Mandi) — Institutional Framework
key_dimensions: Establishment of four markets: grain market (Mandi), cloth market (Sarai Adl), cattle/horse/cattle market, and general commodity market
Role of Shahna (superintendent) and Diwan-i-Riyasat in enforcing price controls
Distinction between market reform as a revenue measure vs. a military supply strategy (link to standing army)
UPSC trap: treating market reforms as purely economic welfare measures rather than instruments of military fiscal management

concepts.name: Price Control System — Commodities and Enforcement Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Fixed prices (daam) for grain, cattle, cloth, and horses — categories and approximate price points
Use of spies (barids and munhiyans) to report violations — intelligence apparatus linked to market control
Severe punishments for overcharging (cutting off flesh equivalent to short weight)
UPSC trap: conflating price controls with market reform — price control was one instrument within the broader market reform architecture

concepts.name: Diwan-i-Riyasat — Role and Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Office created specifically to oversee market regulations — distinction from earlier fiscal offices
Powers of the Naib-i-Riyasat vs. the Shahna in day-to-day enforcement
Relationship between Diwan-i-Riyasat and Diwan-i-Wizarat (finance ministry) — overlapping jurisdictions
UPSC trap: confusing Diwan-i-Riyasat with Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (arrears recovery department) — both are Alauddin-era institutions

concepts.name: Diwan-i-Mustakhraj — Recovery of Revenue Arrears
key_dimensions: Purpose: dedicated department for recovering outstanding revenue dues — distinguishing it from routine collection
Methods used: coercive recovery, accountability of iqtadars for arrears in their territories
Significance in centralizing fiscal accountability — reducing iqtadar autonomy
UPSC trap: mistaking Diwan-i-Mustakhraj as a general audit body rather than a specific arrears-recovery mechanism

concepts.name: Iqta System Reforms under Alauddin — Transition toward Centralization
key_dimensions: Pre-Alauddin iqta: hereditary tendencies and autonomous revenue collection by iqtadars
Alauddin's reforms: iqtas assessed, revenues audited, surplus paid to central treasury (khiraj-i-muqarrar vs. actual collection)
Role of Diwan-i-Wizarat in auditing iqta revenues — 'wasilat' register
UPSC trap: confusing Alauddin's iqta reforms (tightening control) with Muhammad bin Tughlaq's later experiments or Balban's earlier measures

concepts.name: Standing Army (Paid in Cash) — Fiscal Linkage to Revenue Reforms
key_dimensions: Alauddin's decision to pay soldiers in cash (not through iqtas) — departure from norm and its administrative implications
How market/price controls directly enabled payment of a large cash-paid army at lower real cost
Size of army (~475,000 as per sources) and the revenue demand this created — sustainability debate
UPSC trap: treating the standing army as a purely military reform, ignoring its inseparability from the revenue and price control system

concepts.name: Chehra (Branding of Horses) and Dagh System
key_dimensions: Dagh: branding of horses to prevent fraud (substituting inferior horses at muster)
Chehra: descriptive rolls of soldiers to prevent 'dead pay' fraud
These as anti-corruption administrative tools within military revenue management
UPSC trap: attributing the Dagh and Chehra system to Sher Shah Suri or Akbar — Alauddin introduced both, later rulers only refined them

concepts.name: Taxation in the Doab Region — Geographic Scope and Intensity
key_dimensions: Doab (Ganga-Yamuna interfluve) as the primary laboratory for Alauddin's revenue experiments — reasons for selecting this region
Differential application: harsher measures in Doab vs. other regions — administrative logic
Ibn Battuta's and Barani's accounts of peasant distress in the Doab — primary source reliability
UPSC trap: assuming all of Alauddin's reforms applied uniformly across the Sultanate when Doab was the primary zone of enforcement

concepts.name: Elimination of Religious Grants (Inam, Waqf, Milk) — Secularization of Fiscal Policy
key_dimensions: Resumption of inam (grants) and milk (hereditary revenue assignments) by Alauddin — impact on ulema and religious classes
Political rationale: reducing power of the religious nobility and autonomous grant-holders
Tension between Islamic legal norms (sanctity of waqf) and Alauddin's pragmatic state-building
UPSC trap: mistaking this as anti-Islamic policy — Alauddin's own justification was military necessity, not religious reform

concepts.name: Barani's Account vs. Modern Historiography — Source Critique
key_dimensions: Ziauddin Barani as primary source for Alauddin's reforms — his biases (pro-nobility, anti-low-born officials)
Barani's praise for market reforms vs. condemnation of low-born appointees — selective reliability
Modern historians (Irfan Habib, K.A. Nizami) reinterpreting Alauddin's reforms: surplus extraction vs. welfare
UPSC trap: uncritically accepting Barani's figures (e.g., army size, price levels) without noting historiographical debates

concepts.name: Role of Malik Kafur and Later Revenue Extraction in the Deccan
key_dimensions: Deccan campaigns (1306–1312) as a supplement to northern revenue system — war booty vs. regular taxation
Plunder economy vs. revenue administration — Alauddin never integrated the Deccan into his formal revenue system
Impact of Deccan wealth on Alauddin's ability to sustain his army and reforms in the north
UPSC trap: treating the Deccan campaigns as extensions of Alauddin's administrative revenue system rather than extractive military expeditions

concepts.name: Impact on Peasantry — Agrarian Distress vs. Administrative Efficiency
key_dimensions: Debate: did the 50% Kharaj rate impoverish peasants or was it mitigated by stable prices and suppression of intermediary exploitation?
Evidence of agrarian distress: flight of peasants, reduction in cultivation in the Doab
Alauddin's own admission (per Barani) that peasants were left with bare subsistence — policy awareness vs. indifference
UPSC trap: one-sided view of reforms as either purely oppressive or purely efficient — the reform had contradictory outcomes for different rural classes

concepts.name: Comparison with Muhammad bin Tughlaq's Revenue Experiments
key_dimensions: Continuity: both relied on centralized revenue extraction and strong state control
Divergence: Alauddin's reforms were empirical and militarily driven; Tughlaq's were more experimental and ideologically motivated (e.g., Doab tax hike, token currency)
Why Alauddin's reforms were relatively successful while Tughlaq's failed — institutional stability vs. overreach
UPSC trap: conflating the two sultans' Doab policies — both increased taxation in the Doab but for different reasons and with different outcomes

concepts.name: Abolition of Drinking and Gambling — Sumptuary Regulation as Fiscal Control
key_dimensions: Alauddin's prohibition on wine and gambling — stated as moral reform but also as social control over the military class
Connection to broader discipline of the army and urban population — precondition for effective price control enforcement
Short-term effectiveness vs. long-term failure — Alauddin himself later relaxed enforcement
UPSC trap: treating the prohibition as purely a religious/moral measure disconnected from the broader administrative-military reform complex

concepts.name: Legacy and Durability of Alauddin's Revenue System
key_dimensions: Collapse of reforms after Alauddin's death (1316) — why the system was personally dependent and institutionally fragile
Elements that survived: biswa measurement, dagh and chehra, market supervision ideas — influence on Sher Shah and Akbar
Historians' assessment: 'ahead of its time' vs. 'unsustainable extraction' — Irfan Habib's agrarian crisis thesis
UPSC trap: assuming the reforms had no lasting impact — their indirect influence on Mughal revenue administration is a key examinable linkage
